agent-sync:
I was copying the same skill into `~/.claude/skills` and then into `~/.codex/skills`. Twice, every time, on every machine.

<Shot src="/shots/agent-sync/terminal.svg" alt="agent-sync linking skills into Claude and Codex" />

agent-sync is the canonical copy. A small CLI symlinks each skill and agent one level deep into both homes, and leaves anything it didn’t create alone. On a new machine: clone the repo, run `./install.sh`. There’s also `agent-sync push` / `autosync` so design references travel with the skills.

```text
skills/<name>/  →  ~/.claude/skills/<name>
                →  ~/.codex/skills/<name>
```

The weird bit: the agent folders stay real directories. Nested files still work because the symlink is the whole skill, not a file inside it. Codex’s built-in `.system` skills are gitignored so they never get sucked into the repo.
bento:
Compose navigation is a pile of string keys until someone makes it a type. I wanted the type.

<Shot src="/shots/bento/stack.svg" alt="Typed screens stacked, a modal that returns a Uri" />

Bento is a navigation framework on Navigation3 — Mavericks for state, Koin for injection, KSP so the routes are generated. Screens, results, modals, shared elements, nested child screens, screen tracking. A library, published to GitHub Packages, not an app.

```kotlin
maven {
  url = uri("https://maven.pkg.github.com/padamchopra/Bento")
}
```

The bet is that a screen is a type, a result is a type, and “navigate to settings and bring me back a URI” should not be a bundle key you invent twice. Navigation3 was still alpha when I wired this. Results and modals have to be first-class or people fall back to bundles, and then the types were theatre.
biblioteca:
When I started writing Compose, I wanted to see the theme the way a design tool shows a library — live, in the running app, not in a screenshot.

<Shot src="/shots/biblioteca/theme.svg" alt="A live theme: colors, buttons, chips" />

Biblioteca is an add-on you drop into a module. It opens a screen of your components, and you can poke the theme at runtime.

```gradle
implementation 'com.github.padamchopra:Biblioteca:v0.1'
```

It’s a developer toy more than a product. Change a color, watch every button, decide if you meant it. That loop is the whole point; it was never going to be a design-system product.
encryptid:
I wanted a cryptic hunt that felt like a terminal, not a Google Form.

<Shot src="/shots/encryptid/login.png" alt="Encryptid login, salmon page, a small circus of creatures" />

Encryptid is clues in the page, answers in a box, a leaderboard if you want to be seen. I ran it as a web app — Firebase in front, a REST API behind — with a terminal-looking UI because that’s how a hunt should feel.

<Shot src="/shots/encryptid/terminal.png" alt="The hunt as a terminal: welcome back, testuser" />

The software is just the locked door. The writing is the game — and writing clues that are fair but not Googleable is harder than the website. A leftover test login still works: `testuser` / `itis6inmorning`.
github-pr-media:
GitHub has no API for the nice attachment URLs in a PR description. Those `user-images.githubusercontent.com` links are minted by the website’s uploader. Drag it in by hand, or pretend to be a person.

<Shot src="/shots/github-pr-media/terminal.svg" alt="github login, then attach a walkthrough to a PR" />

This pretends. A CLI named `github` drives a real Chromium with Playwright, on a persistent profile so I sign in once. It opens the PR, clicks Edit, attaches the files, waits, saves. Nothing is committed.

```bash
github login
github owner/repo#42 ./before.png ./walkthrough.mp4
```

It appends; it does not replace the body. The installer puts the command on `PATH` and, if it finds Claude Code or Codex, drops a skill so I can say “put this video on the PR” and walk away — which only works because the browser session is already logged in.
habitus:
Every habit app I tried started from a blank list and an infinite streak. Blank lists I abandon. Infinite streaks I fail.

<Shot src="/shots/habitus/habits.png" alt="Habitus: four habits, 21 days each" width="phone" />

Habitus is 21 days, on purpose — long enough to feel like work, short enough that you can finish — with a library of routines other people are already building, so you steal one instead of inventing one. It started as Flutter ([habitus-cross](https://github.com/padamchopra/habitus-cross)). There’s a later Swift version, and a web companion at [joinhabitus.com](https://joinhabitus.com).

<Shot src="/shots/habitus/modal.png" alt="Adding a habit, a category, or exporting" width="phone" />

The cap is the product. A finish line I can hit. The crowd-sourced library only works if enough people are in it, which is the cold-start problem I never really solved.
linear-cli:
Linear’s website is fine. I still wanted something I could type — and something an agent could type — without opening a browser.

<Shot src="/shots/linear-cli/terminal.svg" alt="linear workspace add, linear my" />

linear-cli is a small Python client for Linear’s GraphQL API. Stdlib only, no dependency garden. Workspaces are aliases; Linear API keys are per-workspace, so one key is one org.

```bash
linear workspace add personal
linear workspace add work --default
linear issues -w work --team ENG
linear my
```

Credentials never live in the repo. Config is `~/.config/linear-cli/config.json` with `0600`, or you store only the *name* of an environment variable. Install drops a `linear` symlink and matching agent skills for Claude and Codex. That was the real itch: I was tired of pasting issue URLs into a chat.
mission-control:
I’d leave the desk with a fleet of coding sessions still running on the Mac — tmux, Claude Code, a few at once — and they were gone until I sat down again.

<Shot src="/shots/mission-control/home.png" alt="Mission Control home: sessions grouped by project" width="phone" />

Mission Control is an iPhone remote for that fleet — native Swift, over Tailscale. What’s running, what’s stuck, what I want to say next. The Mac side is the sessions; the phone is a surface. It is not a terminal emulator I enjoy using. It’s a remote for a specific job.

<Shot src="/shots/mission-control/session.png" alt="A session on the phone, with a prompt to Claude" width="phone" />

The hard part is the trust boundary. Tailscale is how the phone reaches the Mac; tmux is how the sessions stay alive. Everything else is just a surface on top of those two facts. I use it the way I use Sideload and linear-cli: when the agent loop leaves the desk, the phone has to be enough.
phere:
Indian weddings were living in WhatsApp groups and Excel. Guest lists in one thread, the photographer in another, the budget in a file someone last opened in March. I wanted one room for that.

<Shot src="/shots/phere/site.png" alt="Phere landing: the whole wedding, finally in one calm place" />

Phere is a wedding workspace — for the couple, both families, a planner, a wedding company. Dates, guests, budget, vendors, invites. The first screen is supposed to answer what needs you this week (send the Sangeet RSVP follow-up, confirm the photographer balance), not list every aunt equally.

RSVPs are by event, because “428 invited” is a number a caterer cannot cook from. Veg, non-veg, Jain sit next to the count. Money stays behind a permission: family can see the guest list and the run of events without seeing what the mandap costs. AI can draft an invite in Hindi or Hinglish, or a WhatsApp nudge for the people who have not replied — nothing is sent until a person says yes.

What I actually sell right now is more boring than the dashboard. You send the list and the dates. In 48 hours there is a page guests can open, one locked list, and numbers you can read out to a caterer. ₹15,000, UPI, that wedding. Delhi NCR and Jaipur first. I still think of the rest as an MVP.
practikality:
The interface was the barrier. If someone couldn’t speak, hear, or see, the phone still could.

<Shot src="/shots/practikality/demo.jpg" alt="A slide from the Imagine Cup showcase" />

Practikality is a three-tier Android app so people who are mute, deaf, or visually impaired can talk to each other — speech, signs, text, and the glue in between. We took it to Imagine Cup. World finals. I was a teenager. There’s a [video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=VhdyqzMQOGE). Microsoft and YourStory wrote it down; those clips live on the [press](/links) list.

The glue was the real problem. Three modes is easy to demo and hard to make feel like one conversation. The stack was Android because that’s what I had. I wouldn’t ship it the same way now. I’m still glad it exists.
shotformatter:
I kept uploading a clip to some website just to crop it, and watching the file leave my machine.

<Shot src="/shots/shotformatter/site.png" alt="Shot Formatter: scene and shadow settings in the browser" />

ShotFormatter is the opposite: a page in the browser, ffmpeg-in-WASM energy, nothing uploaded. Pick a file, apply the effect, download the result. The file stays in the tab.

```js
const file = input.files[0]
const buffer = await file.arrayBuffer()
const blob = new Blob([output], { type: "video/mp4" })
```

The catch is the tab. Big files, Safari, memory — ffmpeg-in-the-browser has edges. That’s the trade for never sending the video anywhere. Live at [shotformatter.com](https://shotformatter.com/).
sideload:
I live in git worktrees. An agent takes a ticket, I get a folder, I want that folder’s debug APK on a phone. Android Studio can do this. I did not want to open Android Studio.

<Shot src="/shots/sideload/popover.png" alt="Sideload menu bar, Pixel 9 Pro connected" width="panel" />

Sideload is a Mac menu bar. Add a repo (the folder with `.git`, or its `android/` directory). It lists the main checkout and every worktree `git worktree list` already knows about. Pick one, hit Install. If nothing is plugged in, it starts the default AVD.

<Shot src="/shots/sideload/worktrees.png" alt="Searching local git worktrees to install from" width="panel" />

Worktrees are discovered, not registered — there’s no second list to keep in sync. The fiddly part is the rest of Android: a JDK (Studio’s JBR is fine), the SDK at `~/Library/Android/sdk` or `ANDROID_HOME`, and a device that might not be there. Merges to `main` cut a GitHub Release; the app checks that on launch and can replace itself.
thomas:
Linear and GitHub boards are for people. I had a desk full of agent checkouts, and no board that knew which worktree belonged to which ticket.

<Shot src="/shots/thomas/terminal.svg" alt="thomas serve, tickets tied to worktrees" />

Thomas is a local-first board. A small Node server, a React UI, SQLite. I look at it in the browser; agents and scripts hit the HTTP API. Tickets, comments, blockers, worktrees, review diffs, live activity.

```sh
./install.sh
thomas serve          # http://127.0.0.1:4567
```

The rule I keep breaking: status should move because the agent moved, not because I dragged a card. The moment it becomes another kanban, it’s just Linear again, on localhost.
vm:
A course project that got out of hand, in a good way. I wanted to know why Vim feels like it does, not just how to use it.

<Shot src="/shots/vm/terminal.svg" alt="VM, a small vim-like editor in ncurses" />

VM is a small vim-like editor in C++ with ncurses: buffers, commands, macros. Not a Vim clone I would switch to — a way to learn why `:w` and `d3w` feel like they do.

The interesting bits are the boring ones. Command parsing, repeat counts, a macro that is just a recorded stream of keystrokes played back into the same loop. Once those parse, the rest of an editor is decoration. That’s also why it’s hard: one wrong assumption in the loop and everything feels off.
whisperz:
I don’t trust most messengers with anything I actually care about. “Encrypted in transit” still means readable on a server.

<Shot src="/shots/whisperz/logo.png" alt="Whisperz mark" width="panel" />

Whisperz is a shielded chat — Android and iOS — built around private meaning private. The Android side leans on Zcash-style shielding; the iOS app is the other half of the same product. It’s still a personal project, not a store listing.

The interesting constraint is the obvious one: if the server can read it, it isn’t shielded. Onboarding, notifications, “who is this person” — all the product things people expect — have to live with that. I still haven’t made those feel easy.
